extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in technology, business and corporate PR scandals (journalists, PR professionals, concerned consumers)
extracted.subtask_description: A timeline-style account of incidents that together illustrate what kinds of corporate behaviour, decisions, or failures produce major PR crises for a technology company; useful for identifying categories of misconduct or missteps that damage reputation. Extracts recurring failure modes and concrete examples from Uber's history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexist or offensive remarks by leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicly expressed sexist or demeaning comments by executives or board members that generate backlash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Travis Kalanick telling an Esquire reporter 'We call that Boob-er' (Feb 2014); board member David Bonderman making a sexist joke in an all-staff meeting and resigning (June 2017). Such remarks often force apologies, resignations, and worsen perceptions of company culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unethical competitive practices (fake rides, poaching)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using deceptive or coercive tactics to undercut competitors or recruit their workers, such as creating fake rides or spamming rival drivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Allegations that Uber booked thousands of fake rides from Lyft and recruiters spammed Lyft drivers (Aug 2014). Also related: internal programmes to track and interfere with competitors (see 'Hell' programme). These actions damage industry relationships and public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized user tracking and privacy intrusions ('God View')
rubrics_metrics.description: Using technology to track users' locations or accessing individual user profiles without permission, raising privacy concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Revelation of a 'God View' tool allowing tracking of users and a manager accessing a reporter's profile without permission (Nov 2014). Such misuse provokes media outcry and regulatory scrutiny over data practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee surveillance of public figures and private individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees spying on celebrities, politicians, ex-partners, journalists or other individuals for corporate purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Testimony that employees regularly spied on politicians, exes and celebrities including Beyoncé (Dec 2016). Surveillance of high-profile individuals intensifies negative press and legal risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Launching pilots or services without regulatory approval or safety readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Deploying new technologies or pilots (e.g., autonomous vehicles) without required permits or adequate safety testing, resulting in dangerous incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: California ordered Uber to remove self-driving vehicles after a pilot launched without permits and cars were reported running red lights and creating hazards (Dec 2016). Regulatory orders and safety failures severely harm credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: False or misleading advertising about earnings/benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Making public claims (e.g., about driver earnings) that are demonstrably inaccurate, resulting in enforcement action or settlements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Uber paid $20 million to settle allegations it duped people about earnings; FTC said most drivers earned far less than rates published online (Jan 2017). Misleading claims trigger legal penalties and reputational harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insensitive or opportunistic pricing during crises or protests
rubrics_metrics.description: Pricing decisions (surge pricing) that are perceived as exploitative or tone-deaf during protests, emergencies, or sensitive events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: #DeleteUber campaign after Uber lifted surge pricing during a taxi protest at an airport amid Trump's travel ban (Jan 2017), reportedly causing ~500,000 account deletions. Perceived profiteering can mobilize public backlash and boycotts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political associations that alienate users
rubrics_metrics.description: Public ties to controversial political figures or bodies that are interpreted as endorsements and provoke user boycotts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Kalanick's membership on Trump's advisory council led to his resignation from the council after users threatened a boycott (Feb 2017). Political entanglements can quickly translate into reputational and commercial costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to address sexual harassment and systemic workplace misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing a culture of sexual harassment, discrimination, or retaliation to persist without timely, effective remediation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Susan Fowler's allegations prompted an external investigation by Eric Holder and led to firings and scrutiny of workplace culture (Feb–June 2017). Such failures damage hiring, retention, investor relations and public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misappropriation of intellectual property and hiring conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Hiring former employees from competitors in ways that lead to accusations of theft of trade secrets or intellectual property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Waymo's lawsuit accusing Uber of 'calculated theft' of self-driving technology tied to a former employee (Feb 2017); implicated employee was fired. IP litigation threatens core business projects and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceiving law enforcement or regulators (use of tools like Greyball)
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing or using mechanisms to identify and evade law enforcement or regulatory oversight in jurisdictions where operations violate local laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Use of a tool called Greyball to systematically deceive law enforcement, prompting a federal investigation (Mar 2017). Deliberate evasion invites legal consequences and severe reputational damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership conduct that publicly insults or undermines stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: High-profile instances of executives publicly berating, insulting, or dismissing stakeholders (drivers, customers, journalists), reflecting poor leadership tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Kalanick recorded yelling at his driver about taking responsibility and blaming others (Mar 2017); he later apologised and sought 'leadership help'. Such incidents can crystallize broader critiques of company values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inappropriate employee conduct during business activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Behavior by employees or executives on business trips or at company events that generates HR complaints or public scandal (e.g., visits to escort bars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Senior employees, including Kalanick, visited an escort and karaoke bar in Seoul in 2014, leading to an HR complaint (Mar 2017). These actions highlight cultural and governance issues and can catalyse internal investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Victim-blaming, privacy violations and mishandling of assault cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Company actions that invade victims' privacy, discredit survivors, or otherwise mishandle allegations of assault, producing legal action and moral outrage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A top executive obtained medical records of a woman raped by an Uber driver, allegedly to cast doubt on her account; the executive was fired and the woman sued for privacy violations and defamation (June 2017). Mishandling abuse allegations provokes intense public condemnation and legal exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic underpayment or unfair compensation practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Business practices that result in drivers or contractors being underpaid or deprived of promised earnings over long periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Uber agreed to pay New York drivers tens of millions after admitting it underpaid them by taking a larger cut of fares for more than two years (May 2017). Compensation scandals harm labor relations and invite regulatory remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delayed, insufficient, or coerced remedial actions by leadership and governance failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Slow or inadequate responses by executives or boards to scandals, or attempts to deflect accountability, which exacerbate crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Kalanick initially took an indefinite leave, then resigned after investor pressure and a shareholder revolt (June 2017); the board and investors played roles in forcing change. Poor governance responses prolong reputational damage.
